question: According to the company lifecycle slide, what can happen once a business's performance has peaked?
choices: It inevitably declines until liquidation, whatever management does
It automatically moves into a new period of growth without any intervention
It must immediately be sold to a competitor or a private-equity investor
It will either decline or be renewed through a turnaround, possibly leading to even greater success (transformation)
explanation: The slide states: once performance has peaked, a business will decline (work out) or it can be renewed (turnaround) to perhaps even greater success (transformation).

question: How does the course define Turnaround Management?
choices: Managing only the negotiation of the debt of a company with its lenders
Managing the move from entrepreneurial to professional management during the start-up phase
Managing the process of transformation from an underperforming situation, through the inflection point, to recovery and renewal
Managing the orderly liquidation of an underperforming company for the benefit of its creditors
explanation: Slide 11 defines Turnaround Management as managing the process of transformation from an underperforming situation through the inflection point to recovery and renewal.

question: Which of the following labels appear on the company lifecycle diagram? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: The lifecycle diagram shows Start up, Growth, Maturity, Transformation, Future growth, Liquidation, Renewal and Innovation. Franchising and Diversification are not shown.

question: The lifecycle slide says that the key is to identify the early warning signs and take prompt action in order to do what?
choices: Protect the dividend until the end of the financial year
"Break the trend" and drive through the inflection point to a new period of growth
Wait for the symptoms to be confirmed by the audited accounts
Follow the trend of the market until the economic cycle improves
explanation: The slide: the key is to identify the early warning signs and take prompt action in order to "break the trend" and drive through the inflection point to a new period of growth.

question: According to the course, how has scoring companies with financial indicators to predict decline performed so far?
choices: It has proven highly reliable and is the preferred early-warning tool
It has proven to be poor, although it may improve going forward using AI / Big Data
It has never been attempted because financial indicators are not available
It has proven reliable for outsiders but not for management
explanation: Slide 13: scoring companies using financial indicators to predict decline has proven to be poor (but may improve going forward using AI / Big Data).

question: Which of the following statements about perceiving the symptoms of decline are consistent with the course? Select ALL that apply.
choices: Management is closer to the business, so should perceive the symptoms earlier
Outsiders generally rely on public information
Non-financial information is always easy to access
Outsiders see the symptoms earlier than management because they are more objective
Financial scoring models have proven highly reliable
Financial information can suffer delays before it is received
explanation: Slide 13: management is closer so should perceive earlier; outsiders generally rely on public information; financial information can suffer delays; non-financial information can give early warning but may be difficult to access.

question: Which of the following is listed among the common symptoms of decline in the category "Financial data"?
explanation: Audit qualifications appear in the Financial data list (slide 15). The other three belong to Management & Staff, Suppliers & Customers and Other symptoms respectively.
reference: Module 1 – slide 15 (Common symptoms of decline: financial data)

question: Which of the following are listed as symptoms of decline in the "Financial data" category? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 15 lists delays in financial information, creative accounting and increasing gearing. Staff fear and frequent crisis meetings are Management & Staff symptoms; adverse image/media comment is in Other symptoms.
reference: Module 1 – slide 15 (Common symptoms of decline: financial data)

question: Which of the following are also listed under "Financial data" symptoms of decline? Select ALL that apply.
choices: Declining performance versus budget / prior year
explanation: All four correct items are in the Financial data list on slide 15; visible management conflict (slide 16) and supplier disputes (slide 17) belong to other categories.
reference: Module 1 – slide 15 (Common symptoms of decline: financial data)

question: Which symptom of decline is specifically linked to family-owned businesses?
choices: Family members selling shares to the board
explanation: Slide 16 lists "Second generation management, in family-owned businesses" under Management & Staff symptoms.
reference: Module 1 – slide 16 (Common symptoms of decline: management & staff)

question: Which of the following are listed as symptoms of decline in the "Management & Staff" category? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 16 lists top management indecision, visible management conflict and frequent crisis meetings. The other options are Financial data or Suppliers & Customers symptoms.
reference: Module 1 – slide 16 (Common symptoms of decline: management & staff)

question: Which of the following are listed under Management & Staff symptoms? Select ALL that apply.
choices: Rapid management turnover, loss of key people
explanation: Slide 16 lists rapid management turnover, lack of professionalism, lack of leadership and declining morale. Increasing gearing is a Financial data symptom; loss of customers is a Suppliers & Customers symptom.
reference: Module 1 – slide 16 (Common symptoms of decline: management & staff)

question: What additional comment does the course add at the end of the list of Management & Staff symptoms of decline?
choices: "... and very often an oversized board!"
"... and very often a weak audit committee!"
"... and very often a weak board!"
explanation: The last line of slide 16 reads "… and very often a weak board!".
reference: Module 1 – slide 16 (Common symptoms of decline: management & staff)

question: Which of the following is a symptom of decline in the category "Suppliers & Customers"?
choices: Lack of investment in technology and human capital
explanation: Slide 17 lists "Financing operations through customer advances". The other options belong to Other symptoms, Financial data and Management & Staff.
reference: Module 1 – slide 17 (Common symptoms of decline: suppliers & customers)

question: Which of the following are listed as symptoms of decline in the "Suppliers & Customers" category? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Payment delays, loss of customers and more supplier disputes are on slide 17. Creative accounting is Financial data; staff fear is Management & Staff; share price movement is in Other symptoms.
reference: Module 1 – slide 17 (Common symptoms of decline: suppliers & customers)

question: Which of the following are also listed as Suppliers & Customers symptoms? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 17 lists worsening terms of trade, suppliers negotiating with banks, factoring of receivables and declining customer service. Audit qualifications (slide 15) and second generation management (slide 16) belong elsewhere.
reference: Module 1 – slide 17 (Common symptoms of decline: suppliers & customers)

question: If the company has a BtoC activity, what does the course suggest doing to assess possible symptoms of decline?
choices: Review the audit report for qualifications
Look on the Web to assess its reputation through customers' discussions, blogs, etc.
Compare the revenues with the prior-year budget only
Ask suppliers for the payment history of each customer
explanation: Slide 17: if the Company has a BtoC activity, look on the Web to assess reputation through customers discussions / blogs / etc.
reference: Module 1 – slide 17 (Common symptoms of decline: suppliers & customers)

question: Which of the following are listed in the category "Other symptoms" of decline? Select ALL that apply.
choices: Increasing availability of credit and funding
Lack of investment in technology and human capital
Availability of credit and funding increasingly restricted
Post-acquisition benefits (e.g. synergies) not being obtained
Big projects will save the day
explanation: Slide 18 lists restricted credit availability, "big projects will save the day", synergies not being obtained and lack of investment in technology and human capital. The two other options are the opposite of listed symptoms.
reference: Module 1 – slide 18 (Common symptoms of decline: other symptoms)

question: Which of the following are also listed in the category "Other symptoms"? Select ALL that apply.
choices: Management believes that market turnaround is the solution
explanation: All four correct items are on slide 18. Staff fear (slide 16) and reporting delays (slide 15) belong to other categories.
reference: Module 1 – slide 18 (Common symptoms of decline: other symptoms)

question: Under which category of symptoms of decline does the course list "Post-acquisition benefits (e.g. synergies) not being obtained"?
explanation: Slide 18 (4 – Other symptoms) lists post-acquisition benefits not being obtained.
reference: Module 1 – slide 18 (Common symptoms of decline: other symptoms)

question: Under which category of symptoms of decline does the course list "Rapid management turnover, loss of key people"?
explanation: Slide 16 (2 – Management & Staff) lists rapid management turnover and loss of key people.
reference: Module 1 – slide 16 (Common symptoms of decline: management & staff)

question: Which of the following is listed among the general indicators of distress?
explanation: Slide 19 lists general indicators of distress including market share, sales, margins, prices, liquidity, dividends, capex vs. depreciation, high staff turnover, unit costs, etc.

question: Which of the following are listed among the general indicators of distress? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 19 includes currency losses, creditor pressure, short term debt and debtor provisions. The other two items are not in the list.

question: Which of the following is a symptom of decline listed in the course, rather than a primary cause of decline?
explanation: Payment delays are a Suppliers & Customers symptom (slide 17). Inappropriate covenants, misdirected advertising and cultural differences are listed as primary causes (slides 24-26).

question: Which of the following is listed as a primary cause of decline, rather than a symptom?
explanation: Poor post-acquisition planning is listed under Poor acquisitions (slide 26). Declining morale, audit qualifications and frequent crisis meetings are symptoms (slides 15-16).

question: Which of the following are listed in the course as SYMPTOMS of decline (not as primary causes)? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Payment delays, audit qualifications and staff fear are symptoms (slides 15-17). Too high a premium paid, misdirected advertising and cultural differences are primary causes (slides 24 and 26).

question: Which of the following are listed in the course as primary CAUSES of decline (not as symptoms)? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Over-capacity (slide 24), lack of market knowledge (24), inappropriate covenants (25) and cultural differences (26) are causes. Creative accounting and declining morale are symptoms (15-16).

question: According to the course, what should the analysis of causes of decline focus on?
choices: The causal factor and its effect
Identifying who should be blamed for the situation
The external causes only, since management cannot control them
The financial ratios of the last five years only
explanation: Slide 20 states that the reasoning "poor management = bad luck" is NOT SO SIMPLE – it is used as a means to apportion blame – and that one should focus on causal factor and effect.

question: Which of the following statements are consistent with the "Causes – General considerations" slide? Select ALL that apply.
choices: All causes of decline are external and outside management's control
One should distinguish internal causes from external causes
Apportioning blame is the main purpose of the causes analysis
Causes of decline are generally traceable to poor management
The idea "good management = good luck, poor management = bad luck" is not so simple, as it is used as a means to apportion blame
explanation: Slide 20: causes are generally traceable to poor management; the luck reasoning is used to apportion blame (not so simple); focus should be on causal factor and effect; internal versus external causes.

question: Into which two levels are the external drivers of decline divided in the course?
explanation: Slide 21 splits external drivers into MACRO (economic cycles, world events) and MICRO (changes in market demand, loss of competitiveness, commodity prices).

question: Which of the following are listed as MICRO external drivers of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 21: micro = changes in market demand, loss of competitiveness, commodity prices. Economic cycles and world events are macro; cost base is an internal operational driver.

question: Which of the following are classified as EXTERNAL drivers of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 21 lists economic cycles and world events (macro), changes in market demand and loss of competitiveness (micro). Over expansion and capital structure are internal drivers (slide 22).

question: Which of the following are classified as INTERNAL drivers of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 22 lists systems and culture (structural), gearing (financial) and cost base (operational) as internal drivers; economic cycles and commodity prices are external (slide 21).

question: Which THREE categories are used to classify the internal drivers of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 22 groups internal drivers into Structural, Financial and Operational. Macro and micro are the levels of external drivers.

question: In the course's classification of internal drivers of decline, under which group is "Culture" listed?
explanation: Slide 22: STRUCTURAL = management, systems, controls, culture.

question: Which of the following are listed as FINANCIAL internal drivers of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 22: FINANCIAL = capital structure, gearing, financial policies. Controls are structural, cost base is operational, commodity prices are an external micro driver.

question: Which of the following are listed as OPERATIONAL internal drivers of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 22: OPERATIONAL = over expansion, over reliance, big projects, cost base, poor marketing. Systems are structural; capital structure is financial.

question: A company's customers move to a competitor and market demand for its products falls. How does the course classify this driver?
choices: External driver – micro (changes in market demand)
explanation: Slide 21 lists "Changes in market demand" as a MICRO external driver.

question: Which of the following is presented in the course (slides 23-26) as a group of primary causes of decline?
explanation: The four groups are: poor management / inadequate information, strategic & operational deficiencies, financing structure & associated costs, and poor acquisitions (slides 23-26).

question: Which of the following are among the primary causes of decline presented in slides 23 to 26? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 23 (poor management; inadequate information), slide 24 (strategic & operational deficiencies) and slide 25 (financing structure) are primary causes. The other two are not listed.

question: Which of the following are listed as characteristics of POOR MANAGEMENT as a primary cause of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 23 lists autocratic, over-ambitious, indecisive, lack of breadth, no vision, wrong skills. The others belong to financing structure, product and poor acquisitions.

question: Which of the following is listed under "Inadequate information => Lack of financial control"?
explanation: Slide 23 lists cash flows, costing / unit costs, budgets, sales / margins, inventories and capex under inadequate information.

question: According to slide 23, what does inadequate information lead to?
explanation: Slide 23 shows "Inadequate information => Lack of financial control".

question: Which of the following areas are listed under inadequate information / lack of financial control? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 23 lists cash flows, costing/unit costs, budgets, sales/margins, inventories and capex. The others belong to financing structure (25), product (24) and acquisitions (26).

question: Which of the following are listed under MARKETING deficiencies in the group "Strategic & operational deficiencies"? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 24 – Marketing: no marketing strategy, lack of market knowledge, no new product development, misdirected advertising, poor pricing policies. Labour costs and purchasing are under Operations; over-gearing is a financing-structure item (slide 25).

question: Which of the following are listed under PRODUCT deficiencies in the group "Strategic & operational deficiencies"? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 24 – Product: outdated products, mature industry, technology lag, over-capacity, price cutting, declining demand, easy entry barrier, low investment.

question: Which of the following are listed under OPERATIONS deficiencies in the group "Strategic & operational deficiencies"? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 24 – Operations: productivity, quality assurance, project control, labour costs, site costs, distribution costs, purchasing. Declining demand is under Product; poor pricing policies under Marketing.

question: Under which heading of "Strategic & operational deficiencies" does the course list "Distribution costs"?
explanation: Slide 24 – Operations includes distribution costs (along with productivity, quality assurance, project control, labour costs, site costs and purchasing).

question: Under which heading of "Strategic & operational deficiencies" does the course list "Easy entry barrier"?
explanation: Slide 24 – Product includes outdated products, mature industry, technology lag, over-capacity, price cutting, declining demand, easy entry barrier and low investment.

question: Which of the following are listed under "Financing structure & associated costs" as primary causes of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 25 lists number of banks, inappropriate covenants, currency exposure and earn-outs for equity. Poor timing re business cycle is under poor acquisitions; quality assurance is under operations.

question: Which of the following are also listed under "Financing structure & associated costs"? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 25 lists secured vs. unsecured, committed vs. uncommitted, short vs long term, unmatched to assets, over-gearing, bonds & debentures, etc.

question: Which contrast is listed among the financing structure issues that can cause decline?
explanation: Slide 25 lists "Secured vs. unsecured", "Committed vs. uncommitted" and "Short vs long term" under financing structure.

question: Under which group of primary causes do "Currency exposure" and "Interest rates" appear?
explanation: Slide 25 (Financing structure & associated costs) lists currency exposure and interest rates.

question: Which of the following is listed as a cause of decline under "Poor acquisitions"?
explanation: Slide 26 lists unclear objectives, lack of information on target, too high a premium paid, highly geared financing, lack of synergy, cultural differences, poor post-acquisition planning, poor timing re business cycle.

question: Which of the following are listed under "Poor acquisitions" as causes of decline? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: All four correct items are on slide 26. Misdirected advertising and easy entry barrier are listed under strategic & operational deficiencies (slide 24).

question: Which of the following are also listed under "Poor acquisitions"? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 26 lists too high a premium paid, highly geared financing and poor post-acquisition planning. Productivity and labour costs are operations items; number of banks is a financing-structure item.

question: According to the summary slide "Causes & Symptoms – In summary", what is usually the case regarding the causes of a crisis?
choices: There is usually a single root cause
There is usually not one single cause, but a mix
The causes are irrelevant once the symptoms are visible
explanation: Slide 27: "Causes: usually not one single cause, but a mix!"

question: Which of the following statements appear in the summary of causes and symptoms? Select ALL that apply.
choices: It is key to have proper monitoring tools to identify symptoms as soon as possible
A single cause usually explains a crisis
A detailed identification of causes is unnecessary in order to fix the crisis
Symptoms are usually clearly visible far in advance, for those who want to see them
Symptoms are rarely visible before the crisis breaks out
It is key to have the right management team in place to identify and implement action plans addressing the roots of underperformance
explanation: Slide 27 states the three correct points; it also says causes are usually a mix and must be identified in detail to understand the crisis and fix it.

question: According to the summary slide, why is it important to identify the causes of the crisis in detail?
choices: To predict the exact date of insolvency
To determine which manager should be held responsible
To understand the crisis and be in a position to fix it
To satisfy the reporting requirements of the auditors
explanation: Slide 27: "Causes: important to identify in detail to understand crisis... and be in a position to fix it".

question: According to the summary slide, which of the following is a key element to address the roots of underperformance?
choices: Having the right management team in place to identify and implement action plans
Waiting for a rebound in the market
explanation: Slide 27: key to have the right management team in place to identify and implement actions plans to address roots for underperformance. Reliance on market rebound and big projects are listed as symptoms.

question: According to the summary slide, monitoring tools to identify symptoms as soon as possible should include which of the following? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 27: key to have proper monitoring tools, including adequate & timely reportings and forecasts.

question: In the Red Motorbike situation, what is the bank's only security?
choices: A pledge on your red motorbike, worth €3,000
A guarantee from a family member
A pledge on the cash in all your bank accounts
explanation: Slide 30: the bank's only security is a pledge on the red motorbike, worth €3,000.

question: Which of the following facts are part of the Red Motorbike situation? Select ALL that apply.
choices: Your cash position is €2,000 across your bank accounts
You owe the bank €10,000 in 2 weeks (loan repayment)
The loan is repayable in 5 years
explanation: Slide 30: €10,000 owed in 2 weeks; motorbike worth €3,000; cash €2,000; projected income €12,000/year; projected expenses €10,000/year.

question: In the Red Motorbike situation, what are the projected annual income and projected annual expenses over the next five years (before risks and uncertainties)?
explanation: Slide 30: projected income is €12,000/year and projected expenses are €10,000/year.

question: In the Red Motorbike situation, the total of your cash and your motorbike is how far from the €10,000 due in two weeks?
explanation: Slide 30: cash is €2,000 and the motorbike (the only other asset) is worth €3,000, i.e. €5,000 against €10,000 due in 2 weeks.

question: In the Red Motorbike situation, which of the following does your banker see? Select ALL that apply.
choices: A €1,000 account handling only part of your income and expenses
Your total cash of €2,000 across all your banks
explanation: Slide 30 note: you use several banks; your banker sees only the debt, the motorcycle and a €1,000 account handling only part of your income and expenses.

question: In the Red Motorbike situation, what do you want to do with the motorbike?
choices: Keep it, because you love it
Sell it immediately to repay the bank
Rent it out to finance the loan
Give it to the bank in exchange for debt forgiveness
explanation: Slide 30: the motorbike is "fantastic", "which you love and want to keep!".

question: Which of the following are cited as business disruptions that call for an operational turnaround? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 33: operational turnaround is needed when the crisis has been caused by business disruptions (loss making activities, inadequate product portfolio, oversized cost structure). Cash crisis, debt and new money relate to financial restructuring.
reference: Module 1 – slide 33 (Operational turnaround vs financial restructuring)

question: According to the course, what are the two main objectives of a financial restructuring?
choices: Replace the management and the board
Clean the past and finance the future
Reduce headcount and sell non-core assets
explanation: Slide 33: "Two main objectives: clean the past and finance the future".
reference: Module 1 – slide 33 (Operational turnaround vs financial restructuring)

question: Which of the following are cited as parts of the need for a financial restructuring? Select ALL that apply.
choices: A cash crisis is anticipated (or faced)
Loss making activities must be closed
Sufficient financing (including new money) must be secured to finance the turnaround plan
The balance sheet must be restructured to get to a viable debt
The cost structure must be downsized
explanation: Slide 33 (need for financial restructuring): cash crisis anticipated or faced; restructure the balance sheet to a viable debt; secure financing incl. new money. Closing loss-making activities and downsizing costs are operational measures.
reference: Module 1 – slide 33 (Operational turnaround vs financial restructuring)

question: What does the course say about operational restructuring?
choices: It is optional when new money has been secured
It should only be started once the financial restructuring is completed
It should be systematic, although too many times it is postponed to address only short term / financial issues
It is only relevant in the start-up phase
explanation: Slide 33: "Operational restructuring should be systematic....although too many times postponed to address only short term / financial issues".
reference: Module 1 – slide 33 (Operational turnaround vs financial restructuring)

question: What is the conclusion of the course on operational turnaround and financial restructuring?
choices: Operational turnaround alone is sufficient to ensure long-lasting sustainability
Financial restructuring alone is sufficient to ensure long-lasting sustainability
A successful restructuring will cover both dimensions, to ensure long-lasting sustainability
They are alternatives: a company must choose one of the two
explanation: Slide 33 conclusion: a successful restructuring will cover both dimensions, to ensure long-lasting sustainability.
reference: Module 1 – slide 33 (Operational turnaround vs financial restructuring)

question: Which of the following statements about operational turnaround and financial restructuring are consistent with the course? Select ALL that apply.
choices: A successful restructuring covers both dimensions
Operational turnaround is optional once new money has been obtained
Financial restructuring alone ensures long-lasting sustainability
Operational restructuring is too often postponed
Financial restructuring has two main objectives
explanation: Slide 33 makes the three correct points and concludes that both dimensions are needed.
reference: Module 1 – slide 33 (Operational turnaround vs financial restructuring)

question: Which of the following parties are listed as sitting around the restructuring table? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Slide 35 lists management, employees, equity, secured debt, suppliers, unsecured debt, customers, Administrateur judiciaire / trustee, judge and government, with advisors assisting some or most of the parties.

question: According to the stakeholders slide, what is the role of advisors (lawyers, financial advisors, turnaround manager, etc.)?
choices: They are neutral parties who sit only with the judge
They represent only the secured lenders
They replace the management during the restructuring
They assist some or most of the parties around the table
explanation: Slide 35: "With advisors (lawyers, financial adv., turnaround manager, etc) assisting some / most of the parties".

question: According to the "Alignment of interests" slide, what do all the stakeholders have in common?
choices: They all want to keep control of governance
They all want to be repaid first
They all seek the liquidation of the company
They all desire to stabilize the company and recreate value
explanation: Slide 36: "…they all desire to stabilize and recreate value".

question: Which TWO aspects does the course describe as challenging in the negotiation between stakeholders? Select ALL that apply.
choices: The desire to stabilize the company
explanation: Slide 36: they all desire to stabilize and recreate value, but negotiating the distribution of value and governance can be challenging.

question: Which of the following are stated objectives of the seminar (what students should understand)? Select ALL that apply.
choices: Different strategies available to save the company (or not)
How the financial restructuring process works
How the operational turnaround process works
How to draft a company's annual accounts
explanation: Slide 3: the objective is to understand why companies get into trouble, how the operational turnaround and the financial restructuring processes work, and the strategies available to save the company (or not).
